Pricing Roof Work Across Chino's Logistics Parks, Former Dairy Land, and Airport Hangars

Chino is mid-transition: former dairy pasture converted to master-planned logistics space at The Preserve, older industrial parcels that predate the dairy buyout, and a general-aviation airport with hangar roofs that don't behave like a warehouse roof at all. Three building types, three different estimating problems.

The Preserve and New Logistics Construction

The Preserve is Chino's largest redevelopment, turning what was dairy and agricultural land into distribution centers and business parks. Roofs here are new TPO or PVC single-ply systems on steel deck, and our work is mostly commissioning and long-term maintenance planning rather than repair. Because construction has come in phases over several years, buildings on the same street can be five or ten years apart in age, which means they're on different points of their warranty curve even though they look nearly identical from the parking lot. We check the actual install date and warranty document per building rather than assuming a uniform age across a business park.

Soil settlement is a real consideration in this transition zone. Land that was agricultural for decades doesn't always compact and settle the same way as land graded for industrial use from the start, and differential settlement under a slab can telegraph into roof drainage problems over time — low spots that weren't in the original design developing a few years after occupancy. When we inspect newer Preserve buildings for ponding complaints, we check whether the roof deck itself has developed a low area versus a drain simply needing service, because the fix is very different depending on which one it is.

Older Industrial Parcels Outside The Preserve

Chino's industrial areas that predate the dairy-to-logistics conversion — closer to the historic core and along Central Avenue — carry an older mix of built-up roofing, modified bitumen, and early single-ply systems, some now three or four decades old. These buildings need the standard layer-count and core-cut analysis before we can even talk membrane options, since California's two-layer limit often forces a tear-off decision regardless of what an owner would prefer to spend.

We see a lot of patch-on-patch repair history on these roofs — small emergency fixes stacked over years without an overall plan. Our estimate separates what's salvageable from what isn't, because an owner deciding between a $40,000 recover and a $95,000 full reroof needs the deck condition and insulation moisture content in front of them, not a verbal assurance either way. Moisture-scan readings on these older roofs frequently show wet insulation well beyond the visible leak point, which is the number that actually decides whether a recover is a responsible option.

Chino Airport Hangar Roofs

Hangar buildings at Chino Airport present a roof geometry that's unusual for commercial work: long clear spans with minimal interior support, often curved or gabled metal roof systems, built to accommodate aircraft rather than racking or office space. Span length changes how a roof deflects under wind and snow-equivalent loading in ways a flat warehouse roof doesn't experience, and fastener and seam detailing on a curved or gabled metal panel roof follows a different install logic than flat single-ply.

We also account for the aviation use itself: fuel vapor considerations near certain hangar types, door-track interfaces at the roofline where large hangar doors meet the roof structure, and access limitations tied to active flight-line operations. A hangar roof estimate takes longer to put together than a warehouse of the same square footage because the assembly is genuinely different, not because we're padding the bid.

Across Chino's building types, our estimate typically covers:

  • Per-building warranty and install-date verification within multi-phase developments like The Preserve
  • Deck-level ponding versus drain-service diagnosis on newer construction
  • Layer count and core-cut analysis on pre-Preserve industrial stock
  • Patch-repair history review to separate salvageable areas from failed sections
  • Span-specific structural and fastening review for hangar and curved-roof buildings
  • Access coordination for active flight-line or logistics-yard operations

Chino Owners Ask Us

Why is my new building at The Preserve already ponding water?

Sometimes it's a drain that needs clearing, but on former agricultural land we also check whether the deck itself has developed a low spot from differential settlement. The diagnosis changes the fix, so we check both before recommending anything.

How do you price a hangar roof compared to a standard warehouse?

Hangar roofs usually cost more per square foot because the clear-span structure, door-track interfaces, and often curved or gabled geometry require different fastening and flashing details than a flat warehouse roof. We itemize those differences rather than quoting a blended industrial rate.

My building has three roof layers already from years of patch repairs. What are my options?

Under current code, three layers generally forces a tear-off; a recover isn't an option at that point regardless of budget preference. We core-cut to confirm the actual count before quoting so there's no dispute once demolition starts.

Are all the buildings in The Preserve the same roof age?

No. Construction has rolled out in phases over several years, so buildings that look similar can be on very different points of their warranty timeline. We verify install date and warranty status per building rather than assuming uniformity.

Do fuel operations near hangars affect what roofing materials you use?

Yes, in certain hangar configurations vapor exposure and fire-code considerations affect material selection and detailing near fuel-handling areas. We review the specific hangar's use and layout before specifying a system.
